new_statements.quote: One exception is Nganyaywana (Crowley 1976:25) where: "The rules for stress placement are largely unknown, but the Nganjaywana forms in the Court notebooks carry stress on the first syllable -how general this rule is, is not known." Forms cited with stress from Court are 'kjaja 'food' (cf. Djangadi wigaj) and 'gwa:Na 'child' (cf. Yugambal gugaNa). These are consistent with a stress-shift analysis, since the first syllable has been lost in its entirety. I suggest, then, that in pre-Nganyaywana stress shifted from the first to second syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand statement (Crowley 1976) says stress placement in Nganyaywana is largely unknown; the few forms with stress marked in Court's notebooks have stress on the first syllable of the attested (already initial-dropped) word, generality unknown. Blevins (second-hand, historical) infers that pre-Nganyaywana shifted stress from the 1st to the 2nd syllable before the initial syllable was lost, so that synchronic initial stress continues an old second-syllable stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Crowley explicitly flags that the generality of first-syllable stress is not known (data are a handful of notebook forms of a language no longer spoken).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolated lexical items transcribed in early-20th-c. notebooks (Court); no phrase-level information. Language dormant; no instrumental or modern fieldwork possible.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to Nganyaywana/Nganjaywana = Anaiwan/Anēwan (ngan1296, AIATSIS D24). The language is dormant; Crowley's phonology rests on 19th-20th c. records (Mathews 1903, Buchanan 1901, Radcliffe-Brown, Court notebooks). The only stress marks come from the Court notebooks; Blevins's 'second-syllable' claim is a reconstruction for pre-Nganyaywana, not a synchronic description.

sources.citation: Blevins, Juliette. 2001. Where have all the onsets gone? Initial consonant loss in Australian Aboriginal languages. In J. Simpson, D. Nash, M. Laughren, P. Austin & B. Alpher (eds), Forty years on: Ken Hale and Australian languages, 481-492. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics 512.
sources.note: p.484 quotes Crowley (1976:25) verbatim: stress rules for Nganyaywana largely unknown, but Court-notebook forms carry first-syllable stress ('kjaja 'food', 'gwa:Na 'child'); Blevins argues these are consistent with a pre-Nganyaywana shift of stress from 1st to 2nd syllable followed by loss of the whole initial syllable; table p.489 lists Nganyaywana initial C-loss as 'invariable' (Crowley 1976, 1979).
